ideas.title: The woodblock press
ideas.critique: Marks that stay where you press them are close to the human's spray-can example, and the mirror-image payoff echoes the upside-down picture in the camera obscura. What is strong is a block you really cut and a print that is pale exactly where the contact was uneven, because the player authors what comes out. The risk is that the 'pressure' is faked as a simple threshold.

ideas.title: Smoke rings
ideas.critique: Rings driven by Biot-Savart that leapfrog through each other are dynamics the island has never had, and few games have them at all. Rings lit by lanterns in the traced volume are a real showcase. The goals are mostly one-off trick shots, and the whole thing rests on the leapfrog actually emerging from the solver rather than being staged.

ideas.title: Leaf boats down the stream
ideas.critique: Water that flows and carries things is almost word for word one of the human's examples, and a leaf race down a stream is the expected way to build it. What is strong is a real shallow-water field with stones the player can move and eddies that decide the race, so it can be played again.

ideas.title: The potter's wheel and the kiln
ideas.critique: A craft bench with a usable product is a known game shape, and an axisymmetric profile is a strong simplification of clay. Clay that keeps its volume, a rim flung out by spinning, and cracks where uneven walls meet heat give a real skill to learn. Traced glazes fit the materials goal well.

ideas.title: Thin ice
ideas.critique: This builds on the frozen sea, but plate bending, cracks that run along the stress field and stay there, and skates that grip across the blade are a real step past a change of material. Cracks drawn as refractive cuts over dark water are traced light a game engine cannot fake. Reading the ice gives the player real risk.

ideas.title: Hide and seek in the dark, by clapping
ideas.critique: This is the third clap-echo post in a row, and its film will most likely show the same spreading ring of light again. The full-scene echo and the owl as a timer finally give the mechanic a goal and a choice worth making, but someone who watched the last two posts will see the same picture.

ideas.title: Sailing upwind
ideas.critique: Sailing is a familiar game activity, and buoy racing against creatures is the plain way to frame it. Tacking that only works because lift really comes from a cloth sail at its true angle to the wind, with a keel resisting slip, is a skill the player discovers. The snap of the sail filling is a strong moment to film.

ideas.title: Bees that tell each other where the flowers are
ideas.critique: Steering a population without touching it repeats the hands-off selection of the breeding pen. Information passed through a dance encoded as an angle, with flowers that refill, is a new kind of collective behaviour for the island. The idea depends on the swarm's shift being visible and slow enough to read, and the honey and smoker part is decoration.

ideas.title: Lumi learns the unicycle
ideas.critique: Balance games with funny falls are a well-worn genre, and 'Lumi gets better with practice' easily turns into a hidden multiplier. A real inverted pendulum with jointed bodies is solid physics to build on. A controller that visibly learns would be genuinely new for Lumi's body, provided the falls do not jitter or pop.

ideas.title: Soapbox carts down the hill
ideas.critique: Build-a-cart-and-crash is one of the most predictable physics-game shapes, and the payoff is the expected crash on the bend. Breakable axles and riders thrown off as bodies make the build matter, so racing again with a different build is fun. Little in it is new to someone who knows such games.
